articles.title: US Open: Sky Sports agrees three-year extension to show the US Open until end of 2030
articles.summary: Sky Sports agrees three-year extension to broadcast the US Open; 2026 competition reaches thrilling conclusion at Flushing Meadows this weekend; watch Aryna Sabalenka take on Elena Rybakina in the women's final on Saturday, followed by the men's final on Sunday
articles.body:
As part of the partnership with the United States Tennis Association (USTA), Sky Sports will retain exclusive live coverage of all men's and women's singles, doubles, mixed doubles, juniors and wheelchair competitions throughout the three-week tournament. The agreement was negotiated by the USTA's media rights partner, IMG.

Alongside broadcast rights, fans in the UK and Ireland will also be able to catch up on all the action with clips and highlights available across Sky's digital and social platforms.

This year's coverage has featured augmented reality graphics, enhanced data integrations, in-depth touchscreen analysis and behind-the-scenes content, bringing fans closer to the action than ever before.

Sky's tennis coverage is led by presenter Gigi Salmon and includes expert analysis from Tim Henman and Laura Robson, alongside additional talent and co-commentators at events throughout the season. Match commentary is provided by Jonathan Overend.

The announcement comes amid a drama-filled US Open featuring the shock first-round exit of 24-time Grand Slam champion Novak Djokovic and the latest finish in tournament history between Ben Shelton and Carlos Alcaraz as the American emerged victorious at 3.33am.

A thrilling women's final meanwhile awaits as World No 1 Aryna Sabalenka takes on World No 2 Elena Rybakina on Saturday.

Jonathan Licht, Chief Executive Officer Sky Sports UK & Ireland, said : "The US Open is one of the highlights of the sporting calendar, featuring the biggest names in both the men's and women's games, all set against the spectacular New York backdrop. We're delighted to extend our partnership with the USTA, reinforcing our shared commitment to embracing innovation, showcasing the best in the sport and delivering world-class coverage for viewers. This renewal further cements Sky Sports' position as the home of sport in the UK and Ireland, offering fans unrivalled breadth and value all year round."

Kirsten Corio, Chief Commercial Officer, USTA: "The US Open and Sky Sports have been trusted partners for many years, and we're excited to continue such a strong relationship with this renewal. Sky shares our commitment to delivering innovative and cutting-edge coverage to a great audience of tennis fans in the U.K. and Ireland, and we're confident that our continued partnership will have a direct impact on tennis' extraordinary growth and deepen fans' connection with the game."

Live tennis is available all year on Sky, including full coverage of the ATP and WTA Tours on Sky Sports or available to stream with NOW and the Sky Sports app. Sky Sports will broadcast over 4,000 matches and 80 tournaments this season.

The partnership extension adds to Sky's already unrivalled portfolio in the UK and Ireland with more top-quality sport than anywhere else, with most sport rights renewed until near the end of the decade. That includes 1,500 games from the Premier League, WSL, EFL and SPFL, exclusive live coverage from every Formula 1 race weekend until the end of 2034, home men's and women's international England cricket, every shot from the golf Majors, year-round coverage of darts, world class boxing from promoters Zuffa and MVP, and more action from the NFL, Netball Super League and rugby league.

The US Open is live on Sky Sports from August 30. Stream tennis with no contract on NOW and the Sky Sports App . You can also watch the Laver Cup at The O2 in London from 25-27 September live on Sky Sports.

articles.standfirst: El partido entre Zverev y Khachanov no ha despertado ninguna atención en Nueva York
articles.summary: El partido entre Zverev y Khachanov no ha despertado ninguna atención en Nueva York
articles.body: Las primeras consecuencias de la ausencia de Carlos Alcaraz en el cuadro individual masculino del US Open (el murciano cayó derrotado el martes en los cuartos con Ben Shelton) se empiezan a notar este viernes en las semifinales. Las entradas, que inicialmente tenían un precio de 300 dólares, se pueden adquirir en diferentes plataformas por tan sólo 19 dólares. Y es que la primera semifinal entre Alexander Zverev y Karen Khachanov no ha despertado ningún tipo de interés entre el público neoyorquino (antes se había jugado la fina de dobles femeninos) y ha dejado vacía la grada de la central Arthur Ashe, la pista más grande del mundo con capacidad para más de 20.000 espectadores. La ciudad de Nueva York vive de espaldas al tenis este viernes, no en vano se está celebrando el vigésimo quinto aniversario del atentado terrorista contra las Torres Gemelas. La Zona Cero cuenta en la actualidad con dos inmensas fuentes con cascadas artificiales situadas exactamente donde se erigían las torres. Se conmemora la fecha con la lectura pública de los nombres de los fallecidos. Estuvieron expresidentes de los Estados Unidos como Bush, Clinton, Obama y Biden. Faltó el actual, Donald Trump. El último grande del curso empezó poniendo a la venta las entradas más cara en la historia de los Grand Slam. El abono más barato de paseo, sin acceso a los estadios, ascendía a 323 dólares.

articles.title: US Open 2026 results: Taylor Townsend and Katerina Siniakova win women's doubles for career Grand Slam
articles.summary: Katerina Siniakova and Taylor Townsend win the women's doubles at the US Open to complete a historic career doubles Grand Slam.
articles.body:
Katerina Siniakova and Taylor Townsend won the women's doubles at the US Open to complete a historic career doubles Grand Slam as a pairing.

The top seeds came from a set down to beat American wildcards Ashlyn Krueger and Robin Montgomery 5-7 6-0 6-2 in New York.

Their triumph at Flushing Meadows means they have now won all four Grand Slam titles, adding to their triumphs at Wimbledon in 2024, the Australian Open in 2025 and this year's French Open.

It was Czech player Siniakova's 12th Grand Slam doubles title in total, while she also became the first player to complete the career Slam with two different partners.

The 30-year-old achieved it previously with fellow Czech Barbora Krejcikova.

For American Townsend, who is also 30, victory marks her first US Open doubles title after suffering defeat in the final last year alongside Siniakova to Gabriela Dabrowski and Erin Routliffe.

Siniakova and Townsend had not dropped a set before the final, but lost the opener when the Czech player double-faulted three times in the final game.

They hit back in the second set, winning 23 of 27 points after the first game to force a decider.

Siniakova and Townsend remained in control from there, consolidating an early break in the third set to go 3-1 up before safely seeing out the rest of the match.

Siniakova is one of only eight women to have won at least 12 Grand Slam doubles titles in the Open era.

Should Siniakova end this season as the world number one in doubles, it will mark the sixth time she has achieved the feat, surpassing Martina Navratilova for the most year-end top-ranked finishes in WTA history.

articles.title: US Open: Will it be a 'three-peat' for Aryna Sabalenka or a maiden title in New York for new No 1 Elena Rybakina?
articles.summary: Can Aryna Sabalenka make it a hat-trick of titles in New York or will incoming world No 1 Elena Rybakina deny her and claim a third Grand Slam?; watch the US Open live on Sky Sports Tennis and Sky Sports+, streaming service NOW and the Sky Sports app
articles.body:
Rybakina's results this year, starting with her Australian Open final triumph against Sabalenka, will see her rise to the top of the rankings on Monday, ending the Belarussian's 99-week reign.

But Sabalenka can exact some revenge for both that defeat and being overtaken at the WTA summit by defending her US Open title against Rybakina in Saturday's Flushing Meadows final - live on Sky Sports Tennis from 5pm.

"I really understand about how tough it is to reach the world No 1," said Sabalenka.

"It's a lot of work and, yeah, that was one of my goals, but right now there was not much I could do. I didn't really perform well in the middle of the season.

"Elena took it over and played really well. But I can only focus on myself and just stay in the moment and trying to do my best right now just so I keep it tight - and maybe I will take it back from her.

"But, yeah, it does feel a little bit weird. You can perform well in the tournament but still lose the number one position. So it's OK. It's sport. I love that. That's the beauty of sport, right? Like, everyone chasing everyone, and it's all about little things that you improve and you get better at."

A mouth-watering final between the two top seeds

Two-time defending champion Sabalenka is looking to become the first woman to achieve a unique hat-trick in New York since Serena Williams in 2014.

It is a mouth-watering final between the two top seeds, the first time that has happened at the US Open since Williams beat Victoria Azarenka in 2013.

"It's an important match, and since it's a final, it's honestly, I feel like it doesn't matter who is on the other side. You just want to win and do your best," said Rybakina, the first player from Kazakhstan to reach world No 1.

"But also, I don't want to put too much pressure on myself because we are all very close in the ranking.

"Even if something goes wrong in the final, I still have other opportunities, other tournaments until the end of the year.

"We push each other when we play these matches, and you clearly can see on what you need to work more. I think that's great that you play against someone who pushes you till the limits."

'This is Sabalenka's house and all the other girls are guests'

Sabalenka admitted earlier in the tournament that she would rather win a third US Open title than retain the world No 1 ranking.

Her performance coach Jason Stacy said: "Aryna is remembering who she is - being very, very aligned with who she is. She knows what she's capable of. She knows that playing someone like Jess [Pegula] on a big stage in a big moment, that she needs to step it up.

"She just has to show up and understand - no disrespect to anybody, is that this is her house and all the other girls are just guests, and it's time for them to go home."

Max Mirnyi, a former Belarusian star who reached a career-high world No 18, added: "For Aryna, we can see that she has been improving as the tournament goes on. We're excited. She certainly fits well with New York. I think she fits perfectly for this environment.

"She likes this circumstance of being the glamour girl and having the spotlight on her, dealing with the pressures of the night sessions, and she thrives in this pressure. That's why she has been successful."

Can Rybakina seal a third Grand ‌Slam crown?

The pair have played two previous Grand Slam finals, with Sabalenka defeating Rybakina in ​the 2023 Australian Open decider before the Kazakh levelled the score at Melbourne Park in January.

"It's an important match, and since it's a final, I ​feel like it doesn't matter who's on the other ⁠side," said Rybakina.

"I don't want to put too much pressure on myself, because ‌we're very close in the rankings. Even if something goes wrong in the final, I'll still have other opportunities and other tournaments until the end of ‌the year.

"We push each other when we play these matches, and you can clearly see what you need to work on more. I think that's great that you play against someone who pushes you to the limit."

articles.title: Townsend, Siniakova win US Open women's doubles title for career Grand Slam
articles.summary: It was a double celebration for Katerina Siniakova and for Taylor Townsend, the final piece of the puzzle to a career Grand Slam.
articles.body:
NEW YORK – It was a double celebration for Katerina Siniakova and for Taylor Townsend, the final piece of the puzzle to a career Grand Slam.

Siniakova and Townsend, the tournament's No. 1 seed, captured their first U.S. Open women's doubles title together, rallying to beat young Americans Ashlyn Krueger and Robin Montgomery 5-7, 6-0, 6-2 in the final in Arthur Ashe Stadium on on Friday, Sept. 11.

Townsend, a 30 year-old American, and Siniakova, a 30-year-old from Czechia, captured their first major title at Wimbledon in 2024 before adding the 2025 Australian Open, the 2026 French Open and this US Open championship.

Townsend and Siniakova found themselves down 0-3, and went on to lose the first set, but then they turned it on, blanking the wildcard entrants in the second set, before slamming and forehand baselining their way to a 6-2 closing set.

For Siniakova, it was actually the second time she completed career doubles Grand Slam, having already accomplished the feat with Barbora Krejcikova when the pair won the 2022 US Open. She has also won a doubles title at the 2024 French Open with Coco Gauff.

"There was lot of nerves," Siniakova said after the match. "We were really fighting for this one, so I'm just really proud. We did it."

Krueger and Montgomery went on quite a run, beating the defending champions Erin Routliffe and Gabriela Dabrowski in separate matches, as both played with different partners this time around.

It was also a reunion for Krueger and Montgomery, who won the U.S. Open girls' doubles title in 2021.

"I think with what we've just done has been amazing." Montgomery said. "I think we did forget that we were offered a wild card, so I'm just glad we made good use of it, and I'm glad we were able to come back together and continue playing here, especially with our success in juniors."

For Townsend, the match served a greater historical marker for black American tennis players. Addressing the fans inside Ashe following their victory, Townsend pointed out that there were two Black American women competing in the doubles final – herself and Montgomery – on the same day two Black American men will face off in the men's singles semifinals for a place in Sunday's final.

Watch: Townsend and Siniakova celebrate with bottles of bubbly

articles.title: Sabalenka vs Rybakina: US Open women’s singles final – start, prize, form
articles.summary: Top seeds Aryna Sabalenka and Elena Rybakina clash in a Grand Slam final for the second time this year.
articles.body:
Who : Aryna Sabalenka vs Elena Rybakina What : US Open 2026 women’s singles final Where : Arthur Ashe Stadium, New York, United States When : Saturday, September 12, 4pm local time (20:00 GMT) How to follow: We’ll have all the build-up on Al Jazeera Sport from 1pm local time (17:00 GMT) before our live text commentary stream.

The top two seeds at the US Open 2026 clash in the women’s singles final on Saturday, as two-time defending champion Aryna Sabalenka takes on soon-to-be world No. 1 Elena Rybakina.

Saturday’s clash at Arthur Ashe Stadium offers top seed Sabalenka the opportunity to complete a rare “three-peat” of US Open titles – a feat achieved by only two other women.

But second seed Rybakina will try to deal Sabalenka another blow, having already ensured the Belarusian’s 99-week reign at the top when the rankings are updated on Monday.

As the pair meet in a Grand Slam final for the third time, Al Jazeera tells you everything you need to know:

Who did Sabalenka and Rybakina beat in the semifinals?

Sabalenka eliminated top-ranked ⁠American Jessica Pegula 7-5, 6-2 in the first semifinal on Thursday, continuing her bid to join Chris Evert and Serena Williams as the only women to win three straight US Open titles.

In the second semifinal, Rybakina silenced the partisan crowd, rallying from a set down to beat 2023 champion Coco Gauff 3-6, 6-4, 6-4.

When did Sabalenka and Rybakina last meet?

They’ve met three times this year, with Sabalenka winning their semifinal clash in Miami and the final at Indian Wells in southern California.

Rybakina won just once; however, it was the biggest of the three, lifting the Australian Open title in Melbourne.

Rybakina not putting pressure on herself before Sabalenka showdown

Rybakina said she will not put extra pressure on herself ⁠before her maiden US Open final, viewing the showdown as another chance to test herself against a rival who pushes ⁠her to the limit.

“It’s an ‌important match, and since it’s a final, I feel like it doesn’t matter who’s on the other side,” said Rybakina. “I don’t want to put too much pressure on myself, because we’re very close in the rankings.

“Even if something goes wrong in the final, I’ll still have other opportunities and other ⁠tournaments until the end of the year,” the 27-year-old added.

“We push each other ⁠when we play these matches, and you can clearly see what you need to work on more. I think that’s great that you play against someone who pushes you to the limit.”

Sabalenka ready for ‘whatever it takes’ to win

The unstoppable Sabalenka pounded third-seeded Pegula remorselessly with her powerful groundstrokes, saying she was “super desperate” to reach her fourth straight final.

“I wanted it badly to go to the finals, and of course, I want to go all the way,” said Sabalenka, who has had a slow summer since back-to-back wins at Indian Wells and Miami in March.

“The mentality was just I’m ready. I’m ready for whatever it’s going to take to get the win.”

“She [Rybakina] is a big server. She really improved over the years on the baseline game, so it’s going to be a physically and mentally tough match,” the Belarusian added.

The 28-year-old has four major titles in her cabinet: two Australian Open titles (2023 and 2024), and two US Open crowns (2024 and 2025).

The Russian-born Kazakh has two major titles: the 2022 Wimbledon title and the 2026 Australian Open title.

Saturday’s final will be their 18th career meeting, with Sabalenka leading the head-to-head 10-7.

It will also mark the third time they will clash in a Grand Slam final after Rybakina won the 2026 Australian Open and Sabalenka triumphed at the same major in 2023.

History suggests Sabalenka is the favourite at Flushing Meadows, having not been beaten since losing the 2023 final to Gauff.

The current World No. 1 has dropped only one set en route to the title clash, and seems to have hit her peak form just before the final in a “last push of the season”.

That said, Rybakina will be no pushover for Sabalenka. Her fighting spirit and ability to stay cool under pressure headlined her semifinal victory, giving Sabalenka a taste of what to expect as the top seeds clash in a major finale once again.

Rybakina, though, admitted that she needs to step up her game for Saturday’s showdown against Sabalenka, whom she described as an “unbelievable player”.

The last player to win three consecutive titles in New York was tennis legend Serena Williams, the champion from 2012 to 2014.

Former World No. 1 Evert also pulled off three in a row between 1976 and 1978.

The winner of the US Open women’s singles final will take home $5.5m, while the runner-up will be awarded $2.8 million, part of the collective $108m the tournament offered at this year’s edition.

The final will be televised or live-streamed around the world by its international broadcast partners.

You can find your regional broadcaster on the official US Open website’s TV listing .

articles.title: Zverev aspira a un doblete de grandes en Nueva York y atrapa a Sinner como número 1 de la temporada
articles.standfirst: El alemán, primer favorito del cuadro, se impone en la semifinal a Khachanov en tres sets
articles.summary: El alemán, primer favorito del cuadro, se impone en la semifinal a Khachanov en tres sets
articles.body: El cuadro individual masculino del US Open tendrá un nuevo campeón y ya se sabe el primer candidato a revelar a Carlos Alcaraz en el palmarés. Se trata de Alexander Zverev, verdugo de Karen Khachanov, por 6-3, 7-6(7) y 7-6(7). Zverev aspirará este domingo a un doblete de grandes en un mismo curso. Cabe recordar que el pasado mes de junio, estrenó su palmarés de 'majors' en la tierra de Roland Garros. Y que después jugó también la final de Wimbledon. El precio a tanta regularidad es que Sascha, ahora sí, es una amenaza en el ranking ATP para Jannik Sinner y Alcaraz. Iguala ya los 7.950 puntos del italiano en 2026. Y, si se corona el domingo, se situará el numero 1 de la presente temporada. Nadie acumula más victorias (52 de las que 24 son en los grandes) que el tenista natural de Hamburgo. A sus 29 años, ha llegado al punto de plena madurez. El partido con Khachanov, el sexto que disputaba en las pistas de Flushing Meadows, era el primero que jugaba con luz solar y lejos de la sesión nocturna que tanto le gusta para poder dormir más. Las gradas, vacías a primera hora del día cuando se disputó la final femenina de dobles, se fue llenando gracias a los precios populares que se encontraban y que ascendían a tan sólo 19 euros. Entre los asistentes estaban los actores Woody Harrelson y Matthew McConaughey,, y la modelo Camila Alves. Todos disfrutaron de la potencia de Sascha y su estado de confianza. Es por ello que fue capaz de levantar dos pelotas de tercer set, con 6-4 abajo en el 'tie break'. Este espera en la final a un tenista local. articles.summary: Alexander Zverev beats Karen Khachanov at the US Open to reach a third Grand Slam final in a row and continue his bid for a second major of the year.
articles.body:
Alexander Zverev beat Karen Khachanov at the US Open to reach a third Grand Slam final in a row and continue his bid for a second major of the year.

The top seed put in a commanding performance to beat the Russian 6-3 7-6 (9-7) 7-6 (8-6).

Germany's Zverev is the favourite in New York after ending his long wait for a Grand Slam title with his French Open triumph in June.

He reached the Wimbledon final in July, losing in four sets to world number one Jannik Sinner.

The 29-year-old will play either eighth seed Ben Shelton or 11th seed Frances Tiafoe in Sunday's showpiece, with the two Americans set to meet in Friday's night session.

"I think it [Sunday] will be incredibly special especially, these two guys are crowd favourites and everyone loves them," said Zverev.

"Tonight will be an epic semi-final and I am looking forward to watching it. Hopefully I can not make their American dream come true."

With Sinner and defending US Open champion Carlos Alcaraz suffering with injuries this year, Zverev has found a consistency that has allowed him to reach all four Grand Slam semi-finals.

He started off the tournament in New York slowly, being taken to five sets in his opening two matches, but has not dropped a set since.

Zverev faced brief moments of pressure against world number 50 Khachanov, saving two set points in the third set, but otherwise remained in control.

"After the second round, at about 3am I was sitting with my team in the locker room and we were laughing at how bad I was playing," Zverev said.

"That sense of humour helped me. I obviously have improved a bit otherwise I would not be in the US Open final."

Zverev won 13 of 15 points behind his first serve and all nine points at the net in the first set as he broke Khachanov to go 5-3 up before serving out the opener.

Khachanov fought back after going a break down early in the second set and forced a tie-break, saving set point with a magnificent backhand to polish off a 22-shot rally.

In a pivotal point of the match, it was Zverev who took the initiative to earn another set point, converting it as he outlasted Khachanov in a draining rally with some magnificent defence from the baseline.

In the third set, both players remained on serve without conceding a single break point to reach another tie-break.

It was Khachanov who settled quickest into the tie-break, opening up a lead and creating two set points - both of which were saved by Zverev.

From there the top seed never looked back, ultimately clinching victory as Khachanov put a forehand long.

After reaching his sixth major final, Zverev stood arms wide in celebration facing his coaching team, before going to the net to shake hands with Khachanov.

Victory means Zverev is into his second US Open final after suffering a heartbreaking five-set loss to Dominic Thiem in 2020.

articles.body: Men’s No. 1 seed Alexander Zverev might have won in straight sets but opponent Karen Khachanov put up a mighty fight on Friday in the first US Open semifinal at Arthur Ashe Stadium. The 29-year-old defeated Khachanov 6-3, 7-6 (7), 7-6 (6) to book his place in his second career final in Flushing Meadows. The match got off to an easy start for the Zverev. He won the first set decisively 6-3 over Khachanov, as the Russian finished with almost twice the amount of unforced errors as Zverev in the opener. But despite the first set loss, the unseeded 30-year-old maintained his composure, forcing a second set tiebreak with Zverev ultimately prevailing 7-6 (7). It was more of the same in the third set with both players going back and forth, trading games. Up 6-5 in the third set and trying to avoid a tiebreak, Zverev went to complain to the umpire about glare from the sun which drew the ire of the crowd on hand. The German went on to lose the game, prompting the second tiebreak of the match. According to the ESPN broadcast, the glare was coming from the glass on the doors of the suites when they are opened. With the issues with the apparent glare still affecting Zverev, he quickly fell into a 4-1 hole but rebounded to tie it up at 6-6 with a trip to the final on the line. After getting to match point by saving two set points, Zverev put away Khachanov and will now look to avenge his first US Open final loss from 2020. It is also Zverev’s third straight grand slam finals appearance, winning his first career major at Roland Garros in early June. Zverev understood his potential fate for Sunday’s upcoming final with the crowd most likely going to be pulling for the winner No. 8 seed Ben Shelton and No. 11 seed Frances Tiafoe. “I think its going to be incredibly special,” Zverev told ESPN. “Especially these two guys, Frances and Ben, crowd favorites here in New York. Everybody loves them. … Hopefully I can not make the American dream.” He will now await the winner of the second men’s semifinal. Up next: An all-American duel between Ben Shelton and Frances Tiafoe On a somber day in the United States, two Americans will go head-to-head in the second men’s semifinal: Shelton and Tiafoe. The showdown is one for the history books for a multitude of reasons. Both are looking to advance to their first career grand slam final, with Shelton or Tiafoe becoming the first American to feature in the men’s US Open final since Taylor Fritz did so in 2024. One of them could also be the first US man to win the tournament since Andy Roddick in 2003. The history goes even further with two Black American men are facing each other in a US Open men’s singles semifinal for the first time ever. And no matter who wins, a Black American man will advance to the final for the first time since Arthur Ashe made his last finals appearance there in 1972. The winner will face Zverev in the men’s final on Sunday at 2 p.m. ET.

articles.summary: Top seed Alexander Zverev out-gunned Karen Khachanov to reach his third straight Grand Slam final on Friday, rolling into the US Open title match with a stra...
articles.body:
Top seed Alexander Zverev out-gunned Karen Khachanov to reach his third straight Grand Slam final on Friday, rolling into the US Open title match with a straight sets win.

Zverev, who followed up his maiden major at the French Open with a runner-up finish at Wimbledon, saved two set points in the final tiebreaker to close out the 6-3, 7-6 (9/7), 7-6 (8/6) victory.

He'll face the winner of the all-American semi-final between eighth-seeded Ben Shelton and 11th seed Frances Tiafoe in Sunday's championship match.

The German predicted an "absolutely epic" contest between the two Americans, after which he'll be out to thwart the winner's bid to become the first American man in 23 years to lift a Grand Slam trophy.

"Hopefully I can not make the American dream come true on Sunday," said Zverev, who came agonizingly close to the US Open title in 2020 before falling to Dominic Thiem in five sets.

After a somewhat inauspicious start to the tournament, spending nine hours and 26 minutes on court in laborious five-set victories in the first and second rounds, Zverev has steadily upped his game.

He needed two hours and 57 minutes to deny 50th-ranked Khachanov's bid to become the lowest-ranked Grand Slam finalist since number 54 Marcos Baghdatis at the 2006 Australian Open.

But the Russian, who fell to Zverev in the Olympic gold medal match in Tokyo in 2021, put up a spirited challenge in the second and third sets.

"Straight-set win, but anything but straightforward in a way," Zverev said. "He played incredibly well, fought incredibly well."

Unable to make any real headway in the first set, Khachanov fell a quick break down in the second.

The Russian couldn't resist a grin when he snuck a passing shot by Zverev to open the fourth game, and flung his arm into the air in celebration three points later when a forehand winner gave him his first break chance of the match, which he converted when Zverev double faulted.

From there, they went to the tiebreaker, where Khachanov denied Zverev on two set points with thumping forehand and a brilliant backhand down the line before Zverev closed out the set.

Neither player mustered a break point in a tense third set. But when Khachanov took a 6-4 lead in the tiebreaker he surrendered both set points with forehand errors. Zverev came up with his 15th ace and sealed the win on the next point when Khachanov sent a forehand long.

"Second and third set I think it's more than obvious that they could have gone both ways," Zverev said. "I just played a few points better here and there, and I'm happy with the win."

A somber note was struck during the national anthem ceremonies of both the day and night sessions on the 25th anniversary of the September 11 attacks that brought down the twin towers of the World Trade Center in New York.

Shelton vanquished defending champion and seven-time Grand Slam winner Carlos Alcaraz in an enthralling five-set quarter-final clash that lasted until 3:34 am -- the latest finish in US Open history.

Having notched the biggest win of his career, Shelton is now chasing his first major final.

So is Tiafoe as they duel to have a chance to be the one to end American men's Grand Slam drought, which stretches back to Andy Roddick's 2003 US Open victory.

Shelton leads their head-to-head, but they have split two prior US Open meetings, Shelton winning in the 2023 quarter-finals and Tiafoe turning the tables in the third round the following year.

The women's final is on Saturday, when Kazakhstan's Elena Rybakina will try to thwart Aryna Sabalenka's bid for a third straight title just days after ending the Belarusian's near two-year reign atop the world rankings by reaching the semi-finals.

articles.title: US Open pays tribute on 25th anniversary of 9/11
articles.summary: The US Open pauses to remember the victims of the 9/11 attacks that took place 25 years ago.
articles.body:
The Arthur Ashe Stadium glowed light blue from dusk until dawn as the US Open marked the 25th anniversary of the 9/11 attacks.

American flags were flown at half-mast as New York remembered the 2,977 people who died when hijackers crashed passenger jets into the Twin Towers in Manhattan on that day in 2001.

That year's US Open had concluded just two days earlier, with Lleyton Hewitt winning the men's singles title.

American player James Blake had lost in the second round that year and was in Augusta, Georgia, on Tuesday, 11 September.

But the New York-born future world number four says the day "shattered the guise of safety" felt by Americans and many professional tennis players.

"It was something that I just couldn't believe could happen in the States," Blake told BBC Sport.

"I don't know if we were all naive, or living under the guise of safety and feeling that everything was going to be OK, but it kind of shattered that for a while.

"There was a lot of panic, at every level - whether it be from the highest of highs in the political world to the people on the ground, to everyone around Ground Zero."

Blake, who would later reach two US Open quarter-finals, was in Augusta for a sweat test, having struggled with cramp during the tournament.

His father, though, was still in New York, where he worked. With mobile phone networks overloaded, there was an uncomfortable wait to discover he was safe and well.

Blake was living in Florida at the time, and with planes grounded, took a hire car from Augusta back to Tampa.

His next tournament was in Hong Kong two weeks later, and he admits it was far from easy to board the plane.

"It was definitely scary because I think you get so isolated in tennis," he said.

"You feel like the little bubble you are in, where you are a kind of travelling circus, is normal.

"And then when you realise how restricted travel can be, it wakes you up a little bit to the reality and how quickly things can change.

"It felt like there was a safety net around you. We lived in a bit of a dream world where you are living your dream of playing a sport for a living, and that can all be taken away."

Many domestic sporting events were paused in the aftermath of the attacks, and the Ryder Cup - which had been scheduled to take place at The Belfry in England later that month - was postponed by 12 months.

In Blake's view, the return of competitive sport helped enormously.

"I think that was one of the things that brought the country back," he said.

"Sports were stopped, but when they came back having [then President] George W Bush throwing out the first pitch at a Yankees game - I'm not a Yankees fan, and I can't say I was necessarily a George W Bush fan - I was almost in tears at that moment.

"It was special to have a sitting president [do that]. And it also signified we are back - we are going to have sports, we are going to continue on with our lives.

"The world seemed like it was back on track in a small way."

There is always a ceremony to mark the anniversary when the date falls during the US Open, and there was a moment's silence before both of Friday's men's singles semi-finals.

Before the night session - and the all-American semi-final between Ben Shelton and Frances Tiafoe - a giant American flag was unfurled on court before R&B artist JoJo sang The Star-Spangled Banner.

"To me it's a really poignant moment," Blake added.

"The 2001 US Open, I remember so well. What would have happened if it happened two or three days earlier, and we were all still there?

"To be perfectly honest, a lot of times I feel playing the national anthem at smaller sporting events is unnecessary.

"But for the US Open, being such an international event and having it around 9/11, I think it is a great moment.
authors: Russell Fuller - Tennis correspondent in New York

articles.title: 158 mph?! Hawk-Eye throws cold water on Ben Shelton's apparent record serve at US Open
articles.summary: The USTA later confirmed that Shelton's serve was only 144 miles per hour — a very respectable number, but not the historic high that the stadium initially r...
articles.body:
Ben Shelton is known for his lightning-fast serve — just maybe not that fast.

During the third set of the 23-year-old's thrilling US Open semifinal victory over fellow American Frances Tiafoe, Shelton appeared to record a eyebrow-raising, 158 mile-per-hour serve, according to the measurement displayed in the stadium.

It was, certainly very fast: Tiafoe was barely able to get his racket on the potentially record-breaking serve, sending the return out of bounds as a result of the rapid speed.

However, 158 mph immediately felt a little bit too high, even for a serve that was clearly hit with a lot of power. That number would have broken several records, becoming the fastest serve ever officially recorded by the ATP.

Unfortunately, the record was taken back quickly, thanks to computer visual system Hawk-Eye. Both Hawk-Eye and the U.S. Tennis Association (USTA) confirmed the serve hit only 144 mph, via The Athletic's Lukas Weese .

The US Open later corrected the mistake on social media.

A 144-mph serve is not nothing: It's still faster than a lot of current players on the tour can hit. But it's a speed that Shelton's serves hit on a regular basis, and it wasn't even his fastest of the night, with the young American clocking a serve at 149 mph earlier in the match.

Shelton's serves, in general, were noticeably faster than Tiafoe: The 23-year-old averaged 119 mph on his serves through the first three sets, while Tiafoe averaged 104 mph. Shelton's superior serve led him to victory in four sets, advancing to his first Grand Slam final behind a whopping 20 aces, including eight in the fourth set alone.

As for his serve speed, Shelton has cracked 150 mph in other events, so 158 might be coming — just not on Friday.

Ben Shelton was excited to see New York Knicks star Jalen Brunson in attendance as he picked up a 4-6, 6-3, 6-3, 7-5 win over Frances Tiafoe in their semifinal match at the US Open on Friday.

"It's not easy playing here at Arthur Ashe," Shelton said after his victory. "You're playing in front of all your favorite athletes and movie stars, so to be able to keep your head down and focus for over three hours is not an easy task. I keep on looking up at the screen like, 'Oh shoot, Jalen Brunson is here.'"

The reigning NBA Finals MVP was spotted at the match alongside actor and director Ben Stiller.

Brunson helped the Knicks end a 53-year championship drought during the 2025-26 season, taking down the San Antonio Spurs in five games to win the NBA Finals.

He averaged a league-leading 28.4 points per game in the playoffs to go along with 46.5/36.3/84.6 shooting splits across 19 postseason contests, which included a 45-point performance in Game 5 of the Finals to defeat the Spurs and capture the Larry O'Brien Trophy.

articles.title: US Open: Ben Shelton is ready to carry American men's tennis out of the wilderness
articles.summary: It's been 23 years since an American man won a Grand Slam title. Shelton is one victory away from ending the drought.
articles.body:
For 23 years, it has been the world's most annoying sports trivia question: Who's the last American man to win a Grand Slam singles title?

Ben Shelton has always been the one with the ability to change it.

No disrespect to any of the others who have carried the red, white and blue banner for more than two decades across the men's tennis tour since Andy Roddick won his US Open title in 2003. John Isner served his way to millions of dollars and a few nice tournament wins. The likes of Mardy Fish and Sam Querrey did the best they could in the Roger Federer/Rafael Nadal/Novak Djokovic era. Taylor Fritz has worked tirelessly to improve his game and continues to be a factor among the best players in the world.

But there is no divine right for any country, even one as big and athletically successful as the USA, to produce Grand Slam champions in a global sport where only a select few are going to rise to the top. It takes everything: talent, development, the right set of circumstances and maybe a little bit of luck.

And for Shelton, the 23-year-old who was born in Atlanta, raised to be an NCAA champion in Gainesville, Florida, and unleashed onto the world stage by a meticulously patient father/coach, only one more match stands in his way of the ultimate American story.

After beating his good friend and fellow American Frances Tiafoe in the US Open semifinals, 4-6, 6-3, 6-3, 7-5, Big Ben on Sunday can complete a journey that tormented so many other very good careers. More than two decades of American frustration is just a few hours of good tennis away from being in the rear-view mirror.

"It's a lot of emotion," Shelton said in his on-court interview. "I'm going to need you guys on Sunday to bring this energy. I'm going for it here. I'm going to leave it all on the court. I hope you guys come and back me. Let's do this for the USA."

Of course, there is plenty of work to do to turn Shelton's dreams into reality. Alexander Zverev, the No. 1 seed at this US Open who finally broke through for his first Grand Slam title earlier this year at the French Open, looms as a huge threat in Sunday's final.

But with all due respect to Zverev, he does not come into a major final with the aura or ability of a Carlos Alcaraz or Jannik Sinner, both of whom have dealt with injury issues this year after dominating the sport in 2024 and 2025. It's a perfect opportunity for Shelton to get a Slam under his belt before scar tissue starts to burrow into his psyche. It's a rare moment to win one of his sport's biggest prizes on home soil and relieve a burden not just for himself, but every generation of American players who won't have to be asked about a drought that went on way too long.

It's a lot to deal with. Whether it's this weekend or sometime in the near future, Shelton is the first one since Roddick with the tools to make it happen.

"I think I've grown up," Shelton said. "I'm more mature, more focused. I know what my goal is. I know what my job is out here and I'm fully committed to those goals."

Until about four years ago, it would have been absurd to predict that Shelton would be the one with America's hopes on his shoulders.

Relative to his peers, he was late to focus on tennis, at one point even preferring to play football. He wasn't on the international junior circuit, where agents and academies scout for future champions. Even in the summer of 2022, when Shelton got invited to play a few ATP Tour events as the recently-minted NCAA singles champion, he expected to return to Florida where his father Bryan had built one of the country's dominant programs.

But when Shelton started to stack his game up against real pros, it emerged almost immediately that he had something different than your typical college player.

Shelton's lefty serve translated into the same devastating weapon that was crushing college opponents. His athleticism at 6-foot-4 popped right away. His borderline cockiness and stage presence suggested that he had the mental fortitude to play well in the biggest moments.

And then, after winning enough matches that he had no choice but to turn pro, Shelton left the country for the first time at the beginning of 2023 to play in the Australian Open. He made the quarterfinals, a result that should have screamed to his home country that they finally had a star on the men's tour who was going to eventually lift one of the sport's biggest trophies.

Shelton's progress from that moment until now has not been completely linear. In his first couple years as a pro, he'd play above his ranking in the majors — his supreme physicality really showed up in the best-of-five set format — but wasn't getting consistent results in regular tour events. He'd flash the talent and the big weapons on occasions but without the consistency to back it up from one week to the next.

Shelton and his father Bryan went to work. Born in Huntsville, Alabama, Bryan Shelton was a solid pro, a classic serve-and-volleyer, but never had the complete game to really compete with the best. After reaching a career high of No. 55 in 1992, he left the tour a few years later and started coaching, leading the Georgia Tech women's team to an NCAA title in 2007.

After Ben established himself on tour, Bryan left Florida to coach his son full time. As anyone who has followed tennis can tell you, parent-child coaching relationships are usually fraught with problems and emotional distress. But when Bryan watches his son compete, his demeanor is always positive, always healthy, even amidst some struggles and bad losses.

As a team, they've taken the long view to keep developing Ben's strengths (serve, forehand, net skills) and chip away bit by bit as improving his weaknesses (return of serve, primarily).

It has resulted in the best tennis of Shelton's life: four tournament titles this year, including the recent Canadian Open, and now a chance to win his first Slam. No matter what happens Sunday, he will leave New York ranked No. 4 in the world and is getting better every year.

"It'll be amazing to play in front of this crowd,, feel their energy, be able to ride that wave. This is a tournament where I'm doing things I haven't done before, breaking barriers I haven't broken before. I haven't had success against [Zverev] in the past, but that doesn't scare me. This is the perfect opportunity to put it all on the line."

It's coming sooner or later. For the sake of American tennis, sooner would be preferable because goodness knows it's been long enough.

articles.title: Ben Shelton beats Frances Tiafoe to play Alexander Zverev for the U.S. Open title
articles.summary: Ben Shelton won the all-American duel with Frances Tiafoe and now he’s the one who can end his country’s long wait for another men’s Grand Slam champion.
articles.body: Ben Shelton won the all-American duel with Frances Tiafoe and now he’s the one who can end his country’s long wait for another men’s Grand Slam champion. Shelton pulled out a 4-6, 6-3, 6-3, 7-5 victory on Friday and will play No. 1 seed Alexander Zverev on Sunday for the U.S. Open title. The No. 8-seeded Shelton had plenty of energy left after ousting defending champion Carlos Alcaraz in a quarterfinal match that ended Wednesday at 3:33 a.m., the latest finish ever at the U.S. Open. Now he needs to stop French Open champion Zverev to give the host nation its first men’s major winner since Andy Roddick at the 2003 U.S. Open. “I’m going for it here, and I’m going to leave it all on the court,” Shelton said. “I hope you guys come and back me. Let’s do it for the USA.” Zverev beat Karen Khachanov 6-3, 7-6 (7), 7-6 (6) in the first semifinal. “Hopefully I can not make the American dream come true on Sunday,” Zverev said. The Shelton-Tiafoe match drew a star-studded crowd that included stars from sports, including Serena Williams, Jalen Brunson and of course U.S. soccer player Trinity Rodman, Shelton’s girlfriend; and actors Salma Hayek, Ben Stiller and Rami Malek. Shelton and Tiafoe treated the fans to a good show, after both had to come through match tiebreakers in the previous round. Shelton, a 23-year-old from Georgia who was less than a year old when Roddick won his title, advanced to his first major final. “This is where we want to be: at the tail end of this tournament,” Shelton said. “This is both of our favorite tournament in the world, our favorite court in the world and to be able to light it up in front of (this crowd) is the best feeling that there is.” Tiafoe fell to 0-3 in the U.S. Open semifinals, the last two against fellow Americans. Taylor Fritz beat him in 2024 before losing to Jannik Sinner. After a ceremony to mark the 25th anniversary of the 9/11 attacks in which a giant American flag was unfurled across the court, it was Tiafoe who played the cleaner tennis in the first set. He committed just three unforced errors to 14 by Shelton, whose double-fault at 4-4 gave Tiafoe the break he needed. But after falling behind, Shelton started serving bigger, and finished with 20 aces. Serving with new balls at 3-all in the second set, Shelton started with a 125 mph serve — Tiafoe got his racket up almost in self-defense and ended up getting knocked backward to the court — and followed it with serves clocked at 144, 139 and 140, the last two for aces that gave him the lead for good in the set. The pivotal moment in the match came in the final game of the third set, when Tiafoe was desperately trying to hold serve. The game lasted 15 minutes and 20 points before Tiafoe put a forehand into the net to end it and move Shelton a set away from the title. Tiafoe had his own marathon in the quarterfinals, coming from two sets down and then erasing a 3-0 deficit in the fifth set to edge fellow American Alex Michelsen. He seemed to get slightly more cheers early, but the crowd was loud for both players as the match went on. Zverev, who had long been considered the best men’s player without a major, finally broke through at the French Open this year. The German followed by reaching the Wimbledon final, where he lost to Sinner, and is 24-2 in Grand Slam matches this season. “Sometimes just things go your way and I feel like I’ve had a lot of struggles at the major level, I was so close so many times, and maybe this year God has said that this is going to be your year and just enjoy the time on the court,” Zverev said. Now he will try to win the title that he still can’t believe he let get away in 2020. Zverev won the first two sets against Dominic Thiem but then lost in a fifth-set tiebreaker, as Thiem became the first man to win the U.S. Open title after dropping the first two sets since 1949. Zverev was solid after going up two sets this time, and has won 13 consecutive sets after becoming the first No. 1-seeded man to play five-setters in each of the first two rounds of a major.

articles.title: US Open: Ben Shelton takes down Frances Tiafoe to seal Alexander Zverev showdown in final on Sunday in New York
articles.summary: Ben Shelton wins all-American duel with Frances Tiafoe to set up US Open final with top seed Alexander Zverev on Sunday; watch the US Open women's final live on Sky Sports Tennis and Sky Sports+, streaming service NOW and the Sky Sports app on Saturday from 9pm
articles.body:
On a poignant evening that began with commemorations marking the 25th anniversary of ​the September 11 attacks, Shelton ‌came from a set down to beat Tiafoe 4-6 6-3 6-3 7-5 and move closer ​to ending a 23-year ‌American wait for a men's singles Grand Slam ​champion.

No home male player has won a Grand Slam singles title since Andy Roddick triumphed in Flushing Meadows in 2003. Shelton will now have a chance to claim his maiden Grand Slam crown.

Earlier, Zverev booked his place in the final with a 6-3 7-6 (9-7) 7-6 (8-6) victory against Karen Khachanov to move a step closer to a ‌second Grand Slam title.

Shelton said: "First, 'Foe' is like a big brother to me. This is where we want to be, at the tail end of this tournament.

"I know what my goal is, what my job is. I'm going for it here. Let's do this for the USA!

"One more thing. It's a difficult day to be out here playing. My thoughts and prayers go to all the families who were impacted by 9/11."

Tiafoe ⁠powered ahead 5-4 ⁠when Shelton produced a double fault, before raising the ‌roof with a hold to bag the first set.

Tiafoe ‌continued to target his opponent's backhand in the second set but serving at 2-1, Shelton thought he had clocked the fastest serve in Grand Slam history with a 158 mph bullet. However, Hawk-Eye and the USTA later confirmed through review that it only hit 144 mph.

With new balls at 3-3, Shelton started with a 125 mph serve - Tiafoe got his racket up almost in self-defence and ended up getting knocked backwards to the court - and followed it with serves clocked at 144, 139 and 140, as he dialled up the intensity to draw ⁠level.

He then broke in the ​fifth game of the third ​set to take a commanding ​lead in the match.

With his booming ⁠left-handed serve and his defence proving impenetrable in the high-octane fourth set, ⁠eighth seed Shelton heaped ​the pressure on late to wrap up an emotional win.

The 23-year-old finished with 47 winners, including 20 aces, to book his place in the title match.

Zverev downs Khachanov to close in second major

The French Open champion had been pushed to five sets in ​each of his opening two rounds but has now won four straight matches without dropping a set, as he reached ​his third consecutive major final.

The victory sent him to his second title decider at Flushing Meadows, after finishing runner-up in 2020 to Dominic ​Thiem.

"After the second round at 3am, me and my team were in the dressing room actually laughing at how bad I was playing. ​That sense of humour helped me," Zverev said ⁠on court.

"I have improved a little ⁠bit, otherwise I wouldn't be in the US Open final."

The German had played all his previous matches during the night sessions, existing in a perpetual loop of darkness and midnight finishes.

The 29-year-old has capitalised on the absence of Jannik Sinner and defeats for Carlos Alcaraz and Novak Djokovic, as well as a kind draw, to reach a third consecutive Grand Slam final.

"I really started off the tournament, and I ​was like, 'Well, this is pointless because I'm not going to do anything here,' and here I am sitting and preparing for a Sunday final," Zverev ​told reporters.

A solitary break was all Zverev needed to pinch a tight first set from his opponent and when he broke again at start of the second, a routine afternoon looked on the cards.

However, a double fault allowed Khachanov back on serve and instead Zverev became embroiled in a tie-break, at one point trailing 5-3 and only winning it after a lung-busting 35-shot rally.

The third set went the same way and Khachanov had set points at 6-4, but two wayward forehands and a Zverev ace gave him match point, which he took at the first attempt.

Rather than fearing a partisan crowd on Sunday, Zverev said he was looking forward to it.

"I think it's going to be a fantastic ​feeling playing, you know, a final in a sold-out Arthur Ashe ​and not in an empty one," he said. "For me, a loud and energetic crowd is always great, as long as ‌they're fair."

Navratilova: There are no asterisks in Zverev's successes

"What a year Zverev has had at the majors. It's been outstanding stuff.

"Okay, Sinner lost early at the French Open and Alcaraz didn't play, but there are no asterisks; he still had to get through even as a favourite.

"And that has given the confidence to play better tennis after that. I think he played better at Wimbledon than he did at Roland Garros, and now he started off badly here by his own admission, but he hasn't lost a set the last four matches.

The US Open is live on Sky Sports from August 30. Stream tennis with no contract on NOW and the Sky Sports App . You can also watch the Laver Cup at The O2 in London from 25-27 September live on Sky Sports.

Ben, un prodigio al servicio, llegó a mandar la pelota a 254 kilómetros por hora, un récord en la historia de los torneos de categoría Grand Slam y el tercer saque más rápido de siempre. El servicio más rápido de la historia sigue perteneciendo al australiano Sam Groth, que sacó a 263,4 kilómetros por hora en 2012 durante la disputa de un challenger en Busan. El flamante finalista del Abierto de los Estados Unidos se sitúa a tan sólo 880 puntos de Carlos Alcaraz en las listas ATP. En el caso de coronarse este domingo, en la final que le enfrentará a Alexander Zverev, la renta quedaría reducida a 180 puntos. Zverev domina claramente los precedentes entre ambos por cinco victorias a cero. Pero la grada de Nueva York tiene mucho que decir.

articles.title: A showdown of Black American men represents progress, and opportunity, in tennis
articles.summary: Years of effort to expand the accessibility of tennis culminated Friday as, for the first time ever, two Black American men met in the semifinals of the US Open.
articles.body: Martin Blackman wasn’t thinking about representation or race when he and his family listened to the 1975 BBC radio broadcast of Arthur Ashe upsetting Jimmy Connors in four sets to become the first and still only Black man to win the Wimbledon singles title. But his parents were. “For my parents, I think, understanding how high the barriers were in terms of the lack of accessibility to tennis in the US, they understood what an achievement that was for Arthur. They also understood the gravity of how poised he was in representing himself and opening doors for other African Americans, and I think that was very compelling for them,” Blackman, now 56, told CNN Sports. “I was just a five-year-old listener.” All he knew at that time was that tennis became the family’s sport. Ashe’s success as a Black man on a big stage had played some small role in Blackman’s introduction to the sport that would shape his life. “And then, along the way, I’ve had people open doors and give me opportunities that I never would have been able to afford. So I’m very blessed in that respect,” Blackman said. “That’s why I love doing what I’m doing.” For ten years that meant serving as the general manager of player development at the USTA, where he “tried to be really intentional with that entry-level programming to make sure that we were getting the widest, most diverse cohort of juniors.” But it was before that - during his first stint working at the Junior Tennis Champions Center in College Park, Maryland - that Blackman met Frances Tiafoe. Tiafoe was six when Blackman started as the director at JTCC, already a couple years into a now oft-cited origin story. Tiafoe’s father, an immigrant from Sierra Leone, worked on the construction of the center, moved into a maintenance role, and raised his twin boys Frances and Franklin on and around the courts. When their mother, a nurse also from Sierra Leone, worked night shifts, the boys would sleep in a storage room. “When he was seven, eight [years old], I would see him hitting on the wall whenever he had free time. I would see him watching other coaches give private [lessons] whenever he had free time, just kind of looking and studying,” Blackman said of a young Tiafoe. And sometimes, if a group of seniors was short a player for their doubles match, an elementary-aged Tiafoe would step in. “So you’d see Frances at seven or eight playing with three other 70-year-old guys, who have the worst technique in the world,” Blackman said laughing. “But he’s learning the game from the ground up in his mind.” Ahead of this season, Tiafoe remade that game, returning to the same grounds where he learned it the first time. Blackman is back at JTCC, too, having returned as the CEO. A few months ago, they celebrated together at JTCC when Tiafoe’s charitable fund, which works to provide tennis and academic programs to underserved communities, surpassed a million dollars. It’s a pillar in primarily his own legacy, but also that of the broader initiative to expand the accessibility and, as a result, diversity of tennis. That effort reached a new culmination of sorts Friday night at Arthur Ashe Stadium, when Tiafoe faced off against Ben Shelton – the first time two Black American men played in the semifinals of the US Open and a guarantee that the finals would feature a Black American man for the first time since Ashe himself in 1972. The work on the court had paid off, as well. Tiafoe slimmed down, redoubled his focus, and saw his ranking rise from No. 34 to No. 12 over the course of this season. But on Friday night, he ultimately seemed to be overmatched by the sustained athleticism of Shelton, waning while the younger man outlasted and outserved him. Tiafoe won the first set. Shelton the second. And then, with Shelton up 5-3 in the third set, the two embarked on a 15-minute game that went deuce seven times before Shelton clinched the set on an unforced error. The very next game, the first of the fourth set, went to deuce three times. Shelton won that one, too. The momentum was officially in his favor. It would continue to be a battle from there, but one with Shelton setting the pace, and Tiafoe faltering. He lost when he double-faulted on what would be his final serve of the night. In his post-match comments to ESPN, Shelton, having punched a ticket to his first Grand Slam final at 23 years old, called the 28-year-old Tiafoe “like a big brother.” The comment was a reflection of their friendship, forged on the tour. But it also spoke to the history they now share as Black men succeeding at tennis’s highest level. Before the match, Blackman considered how it might be viewed by young Black boys, or their parents, and whether it might inspire the next generation of participation from people like him. “I guarantee it’s going to happen 100 different times in 100 different places,” he said, “because these guys, I mean, these guys are so compelling. What kid wouldn’t watch this and say, ‘Oh my goodness, I want to do that.’”

The American believes greater consistency has helped him make his breakthrough in New York.Shelton defeated fellow American Frances Tiafoe 4-6, 6-3, 6-3, 7-5 on Friday (local time) to book a place in the final against top seed Alexander Zverev of Germany.The 23-year-old is now one win away from ending the United States’ 23-year wait for a men’s singles Grand Slam champion since Andy Roddick won the US Open in 2003. He is also aiming to become the first Black American man to win the US Open title since Arthur Ashe in 1968. Shelton, however, is still looking for his first win over Zverev in their sixth meeting."This whole tournament at this point has been unchartered territory," Shelton told reporters, as quoted by news agency Reuters. I'm just excited to put it all out on the line.""I can think about how cool this moment is and what I'm playing for. articles.title: Ben Shelton Pauses Historic US Open Celebration for Powerful 9/11 Message
articles.summary: Ben Shelton paused his US Open celebration to honor families impacted by 9/11 after reaching his first Grand Slam final. The post Ben Shelton Pauses Historic...
articles.body:
Ben Shelton had every reason to make the moment about himself.

He had just beaten Frances Tiafoe, 4-6, 6-3, 6-3, 7-5, inside Arthur Ashe Stadium to reach the first Grand Slam final of his career. At 23, Shelton had also become the first Black American man to reach the U.S. Open singles final since Arthur Ashe in 1972.

Then he shifted the spotlight somewhere else.

On the 25th anniversary of the Sept. 11 attacks, Shelton used his on-court interview Friday night to acknowledge the families still carrying the weight of one of New York's darkest days.

"One more thing, it's a difficult day to be out here playing," Shelton told the crowd . "My thoughts and prayers go out to all the families who were impacted by 9/11."

He then looked around the stadium and added a tribute to the city hosting the biggest tournament of his life.

"This is one of the greatest cities in the world," Shelton said, calling Sept. 11 "one of the biggest tragedies."

For a few moments, the celebration gave way to remembrance.

Ben Shelton Honors New York on 25th Anniversary of 9/11

The timing made Shelton's words resonate beyond tennis.

Friday marked exactly 25 years since the Sept. 11, 2001, terrorist attacks killed nearly 3,000 people in New York, at the Pentagon and near Shanksville, Pennsylvania. Memorial ceremonies were held throughout the day, including the annual reading of victims' names at the World Trade Center site.

By the time Shelton and Tiafoe walked onto Ashe for the night semifinal, the date already carried an emotional weight across New York.

Shelton's acknowledgment came naturally, and importantly, after the biggest victory of his career.

He had spent more than three hours trading momentum with Tiafoe before finally breaking through late in the fourth set. The win sent Shelton into Sunday's final against Alexander Zverev and put him one match away from becoming the first American man to win a Grand Slam singles title since Andy Roddick at the 2003 U.S. Open.

Shelton Calls on American Crowd for Sunday Final

Before his Sept. 11 tribute, Shelton also made one request of the crowd.

"I'm going to need you guys on Sunday to bring the energy," he said. "I'm going for it here. I'm going to leave it all on the court."

Then came the line that brought Arthur Ashe Stadium back to full volume.

It was vintage Shelton — emotional, direct and fully engaged with a crowd that has increasingly adopted him during this run.

But the final words of his interview carried a different tone.

On a night when Shelton made history of his own, he understood that New York was remembering something much bigger.

And before leaving the court, he made sure to say so.

articles.title: Ben Shelton Dealt Bad News Before US Open Final vs Alexander Zverev
articles.summary: Ben Shelton's odds of beating Alexander Zverev in Sunday's US Open final aren't very promising -- and here's why. The post Ben Shelton Dealt Bad News Before...
articles.body:
Ben Shelton is one win away from becoming the first American man to win a Grand Slam title since Andy Roddick in 2003. Unfortunately, his odds of beating Alexander Zverev in Sunday's US Open final aren't very promising.

Shelton has a 0-5 career head-to-head record against Zverev, having lost to the German on five separate occasions since their first encounter at the Cincinnati Masters in 2024. Since that initial meeting, the southpaw has lost in straight sets every single time to Zverev, including last year's Nitto ATP Finals and Cincinnati Masters. Shelton also lost to Zverev at Stuttgart and Munich last year, the latter of which was the tourney final.

Even more concerning for Shelton is that he's 0-3 on hard courts against Zverev, with only one of those matches going to a deciding third set.

The one silver lining, however, is that Shelton was similarly 0-3 against reigning US Open champion Carlos Alcaraz ahead of their quarterfinal earlier this week. Shelton proved his doubters wrong by upsetting Alcaraz, securing the biggest victory of his career and his first against a top-three player.

Ben Shelton's Girlfriend Unlikely to Attend

Another bit of bad news for Shelton is that his girlfriend, Washington Spirit striker Trinity Rodman, is unlikely to attend the US Open final due to a scheduling conflict. On Sunday, Rodman and the Spirit are scheduled to face Boston Legacy FC in an away game in Boston, with the NWSL game kicking off off at 1 p.m. local time. Elsewhere in New York, Shelton's US Open final will start just an hour later at 2 p.m. in New York.

Unless she skips her NWSL commitment, Rodman will likely miss the biggest match of her boyfriend's blossoming career.

It will be a shame if Rodman won't be in Shelton's corner on Sunday. She has been his lucky charm through his excellent 2026 season, which includes four ATP title wins in Montreal, Stuttgart, Munich and Dallas. After his Stuttgart win, he thanked her for traveling the globe to support him—even at tournaments where WAGs rarely show up.

Shelton was smiling ear to ear after beating Frances Tiafoe, 4-6, 6-3, 6-3, 7-5, in Friday's semifinal to advance to his first career major final.

"It's a lot of emotion. My mom and dad sacrificed a lot for me to be in this position today," Shelton said after reaching the US Open final, via Tennis Letter.

"My dad lost his mom earlier this year. She's the reason he was able to play tennis. Without her there's no Ben Shelton standing here today. This one is for her.

"Ima need you guys on Sunday to bring the energy," he continued. "We're going for it here. Ima leave it all on the court. I hope you guys come and back me.

He also dedicated his win to the 9/11 victims on the 25th anniversary of the tragedy.

"Let's do this for the USA. One more thing, it's a difficult day to be out here playing. My thoughts and prayers go out to all families who are impacted by 9/11.

"This is one of the greatest cities in the world and one of the biggest tragedies. Thoughts and prayers to everyone involved and affected."

articles.title: US Open final 2026: Why Aryna Sabalenka has extra motivation to beat Elena Rybakina in New York
articles.summary: Aryna Sabalenka has lost the world number one ranking to Elena Rybakina - but has the chance to take revenge in the US Open final.
articles.body:
Aryna Sabalenka was fully aware she would have to win the US Open to stand any chance of stopping Elena Rybakina overtaking her as world number one.

Even that would not necessarily be enough. And as the pair prepare to meet in Saturday's final, Sabalenka knows her 99-week stay at the top of the world rankings is at an end.

Kazakhstan's Rybakina is assured of replacing Sabalenka at the top of the rankings, guaranteeing that by reaching the semi-finals.

Having also beaten the Belarusian to win this year's Australian Open title, Rybakina now has the opportunity to inflict further damage.

But that provides extra motivation for Sabalenka before their fourth meeting of the year.

"It is going to be red rag to a bull for her - she is not going to be happy," said former British number one Annabel Croft on BBC Radio 5 Live.

"Now she has the opportunity to end this year on a high."

Sabalenka, who has beaten Rybakina in Indian Wells and Miami since the Melbourne final, still has history in her sights as she bids to become only the third woman in the Open era to win the New York singles title three years in a row.

The four-time Grand Slam champion's victory over American third seed Jessica Pegula in the semi-finals was her finest display in months, playing with a fire and freedom that had been missing previously.

Afterwards, Sabalenka played down the significance of losing her ranking, joking she did not care about it.

But she clearly does. Sabalenka's coach Anton Dubrov said as much when he spoke about how the issue has been hanging over her.

"I actually like this [losing the ranking] happened. It's ended and it's extra fuel," Dubrov said.

"There is no more extra draining [of mental energy] or thinking about it.

"There's a next chapter right now. You have to chase again. It's extra motivation for you. Just go and get it."

Sabalenka might have arrived in New York as the two-time defending champion, but there were concerns about her game and mindset.

Over the past five months, the 28-year-old had lost a series of matches from strong positions against opponents she was expected to beat.

The most notable was in the French Open quarter-finals. Sabalenka held a commanding set and a double break lead against 25th seed Diana Shnaider before capitulating to a 3-6 7-5 6-0 defeat.

Earlier in the clay-court season, Sabalenka blew six match points against Hailey Baptiste in Madrid and let slip a first-set lead over Sorana Cirstea in Rome, demonstrating a lack of mental focus that she had not shown on the WTA Tour for a long time.

A chink of vulnerability was still apparent during this North American hard-court swing, when she held clear advantages against 20-year-old Czech opponent Sara Bejlek at the Cincinnati Open before losing in straight sets.

But there was no panic for Sabalenka or her team, says her high performance coach Jason Stacy.

"We all understand that this is just part of the thing," Stacy said.

"We just give her space to be herself, help her figure out what might work for her right now.

"Giving her that freedom, but also knowing that she has the guidance of all of us, I think that just gives her a power that few are lucky enough to have."

For different reasons, two-time major champion Rybakina also came into the US Open with serious doubts about her chances.

Turning her ankle during the Cincinnati quarter-finals left the 27-year-old unable to walk for several days afterwards and put her chances of even competing at Flushing Meadows in jeopardy.

However, not only was the 2022 Wimbledon champion able to play, but she cruised through her opening four matches thanks to a huge service game which rarely allowed opponents to get into points.

Rybakina's past two wins against China's Zheng Qinwen and home favourite Coco Gauff proved she has the durability - in baseline exchanges and physical scraps - to withstand pressure.

"She wasn't even hitting balls three weeks ago," Croft said.

"What was interesting is that she said she worked on other things with her team and talked a lot and did a lot of work without hitting tennis balls.

"I presume she meant mental preparation and she has brought the freshness into this tournament."

By overcoming their pre-tournament concerns, Sabalenka and Rybakina have underlined their position as the two standout players on the WTA Tour.

The pair contesting the US Open final means they will close the Grand Slam season as they began it in the Australian Open's showpiece match.

"Talking about Grand Slams, it feels like a last push of the season," Sabalenka, who is aiming for her first major title of 2026, added.

"The mentality is just 'I'm ready'. I'm ready for whatever it's going to take to get the win."
